newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS--Novartis gene labeling seen changing little.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--Novartis gene labeling seen changing little.

text.p: Novartis AG has taken a major step in supporting labeling of genetically altered crops, but officials of the Swiss pharmaceuticals giant conceded on Monday that consumers may still not know if end products come from gene-altered crops.
"It's not up to us to tell our customers what they should be doing," Wolfgang Samo, head of agribusiness at Swiss-based Novartis, told reporters on a conference call.
"We give our customers the opportunity...to make the decison whether he wants to label or not," Samo said.
"We think that for scientific or safety reasons, there is nothing to hide," Samo said.

When genetically engineered corn and soybean seeds were introduced in the United States last year, opponents -- particularly those in Europe -- demanded that they be labeled amid concerns about food safety.

Agribusiness groups have opposed the practice, saying it was unnecessary and would increase costs because genetically engineered crops would somehow have to be separated from non-genetically engineered crops throughout the food chain.
Novartis on Monday said it would at least label its seed.

"We think that these products are overall superior to conventional ones; otherwise, we would not have a market," Samo said. "Industry should thus have many reasons to label these products, and Novartis is doing this."

Novartis already labels its genetically engineered "Bt corn" seed, designed to create plants that withstand the European corn borer insect. Samo said Novartis may introduce a rootworm-resistant corn seed by the year 2000.
Novartis last month also received the first U.S. patent to produce genetically altered wheat.
Samo told reporters Novartis believed in the consumer's right to choose and he said the industry could not "reasonably argue" against labels facilitating this choice.
But he also said Novartis could not make the decision to label the end-product that makes its way through the marketing chain to grocery store shelves or to livestock feedyards.
That decision was left up to "our customers' customers' customer," Samo said.
Opponents of genetically altered crops reacted with skepticism to Novartis' announcement.
"It sounds like smoke and mirrors," said Beth Fitzgerald, a spokesperson for environmental group Greenpeace in Chicago.

"When they say they support consumers' right to choose, they're talking about the farmers they heavily lobby to buy their product. It sounds to me like they're playing games with the whole concept of consumers' right to choose," she said.

Last year, Novartis sold Bt corn to farmers in the United States and Canada. This year, Novartis plans to sell the seeds in Europe, although last week France imposed regulations that will prevent French farmers from sowing Bt corn in 1997.
Novartis had not yet calculated the costs of labeling, if applied to all sectors of the food industry.
"It can be said that if the consumer wants to have that label, it most certainly will be at a higher cost," Samo said.
Samo said Bt corn may some day comprise 50 percent of U.S. corn acreage, since that was roughly the amount of acreage affected by the European corn borer.
((--Kansas City bureau, 816 561-8671))
